objectives: Walk through the 10 steps of an outbreak investigation.
Apply line lists + epi curves + attack-rate tables.
Distinguish reportable disease + syndromic + sentinel surveillance.

slides.title: Outbreak investigation: the 10-step framework
slides.body:
When an outbreak is reported, public-health epidemiologists follow a standardized investigation framework (CDC's '10 steps'):

1. **Prepare for fieldwork** (logistics, IRB if research, multidisciplinary team).
2. **Establish the existence of an outbreak** — is the observed count above expected baseline?
3. **Verify the diagnosis** — confirm cases via lab testing, clinical criteria.
4. **Construct a working case definition** — clinical + lab + temporal + geographic.
5. **Find cases systematically + record information** (line list).
6. **Perform descriptive epidemiology** (epi curve, place, person).
7. **Develop hypotheses** about source + mode of transmission.
8. **Evaluate hypotheses analytically** (cohort or case-control study).
9. **Refine hypotheses + carry out additional studies** (environmental, lab, food chain).
10. **Implement control + prevention measures**; **communicate findings**.

Classic example: a chipotle Salmonella outbreak. (1) Local restaurant cluster reported; (2) cases exceed expected; (3) lab confirms Salmonella serotype; (4) define a case (specific PFGE pattern); (5) interview affected patrons; (6) plot cases over time + location; (7) hypothesize specific food item; (8) case-control: cases ate item X more than controls (OR > 5); (9) trace item X to supplier + farm; (10) recall + closure.

slides.title: Line lists + attack-rate tables
slides.body:
A **line list** is a row-per-case data structure: ID, date of onset, age, sex, geography, exposures, clinical, outcome. The investigation's central artifact.

From the line list you build:
• **Epi curves** (cases by date of onset).
• **Attack-rate tables**: cross-tabulate cases vs total exposed for each suspected exposure.

**Attack-rate** for an exposure: cases-among-exposed / total-exposed. Comparing across exposures identifies the likely source.

Example table (foodborne):
```
Food      Ill among ate   Ill among didn't eat   AR (ate)   AR (didn't)   RR
Chicken     30/50             5/30                 60%        17%         3.6
Salad        8/40            27/40                 20%        68%         0.3
Dessert     15/30            20/50                 50%        40%         1.25
```
Chicken has high AR among eaters + low AR among non-eaters ⇒ likely source. Salad shows protective association (lower AR among eaters) — likely a non-causal correlation (people who ate salad ate less chicken). 

This 'cohort study within the outbreak' design is fast + powerful for foodborne / point-source outbreaks where a small population is exposed at a known event.

slides.title: Modern surveillance systems
slides.body:
**Surveillance** = ongoing systematic collection, analysis, + dissemination of health data for public health action.

Types:
• **Notifiable / reportable disease surveillance**: clinicians + labs report specific diseases (TB, HIV, measles, syphilis, etc.) to health departments. List varies by jurisdiction; CDC's nationally notifiable lists are coordinated through CSTE.
• **Sentinel surveillance**: select sites report on common conditions (ILI from sentinel providers, influenza-like illness through ILINet).
• **Syndromic surveillance**: ED chief complaints, OTC drug sales, school absenteeism, web search queries — leading indicators not requiring diagnosis.
• **Genomic surveillance**: routine sequencing of pathogens (SARS-CoV-2 variants, flu strain selection for vaccine, foodborne outbreak fingerprinting). GISAID, PulseNet.
• **Wastewater surveillance**: detect viral RNA in sewage. Leading indicator (people shed before symptomatic). Active for COVID, polio, RSV.
• **Mortality surveillance**: excess deaths above expected baselines. Key for detecting under-counted outbreaks.

Modern public-health relies on **multi-stream surveillance**: combine signals from many sources to triangulate. The CDC's CFA (Center for Forecasting + Outbreak Analytics) was created post-COVID to coordinate these streams.

**Privacy + data-sharing** tensions are persistent. Sharing person-level data has legal + ethical constraints (HIPAA, GDPR); aggregate dashboards (CDC COVID Data Tracker) balance access with privacy.

question.question: Walk through an outbreak investigation: a hepatitis A cluster at a college dining hall
question.goal: 30 students at a college developed jaundice + lab-confirmed hepatitis A in early November. Cases were students who ate at the central dining hall.

steps.prompt: Step 1-2: confirm outbreak + verify diagnoses. Background US hepatitis A rate ~0.5 per 100K per year. The college has 5,000 students. Is 30 cases over a month above expected?
steps.reveal: Expected ~0.02 cases/month. Observed: 30. Ratio ~1500×. Clearly outbreak. Lab confirmation (anti-HAV IgM positive) verifies diagnoses.

steps.prompt: Step 4: develop a case definition. What's a reasonable one?

acceptedAnswers: lab-confirmed hep A + dining hall exposure
anti-HAV IgM positive + symptoms onset Oct-Nov

hints: Combine clinical + lab + temporal + spatial criteria.
steps.reveal: Confirmed case: jaundice or transaminase elevation + anti-HAV IgM positive + symptom onset between Oct 1 + Nov 30, in a student / staff / regular patron of the central dining hall. Probable: clinical illness without lab. Suspected: jaundice without specific exposure. Tiered case definitions balance sensitivity (don't miss real cases) vs specificity (don't pollute with false positives).

steps.prompt: Step 6: plot the epi curve. Cases (date of onset) are: 10/15 (1), 10/22 (2), 10/29 (5), 11/5 (12), 11/12 (8), 11/19 (2). What shape does this suggest?
steps.motivation: Compare to common-source point vs propagated.
hints: The curve has one peak followed by decay — consistent with a single exposure event.
steps.reveal: Common-source point. The rise + decay span ~5 weeks. Hep A incubation period is 15-50 days; so the source exposure was 2-7 weeks before the peak — roughly mid-October. A single contaminated event around then is likely.

steps.prompt: Step 7-8: hypothesis + analysis. Interviews of cases reveal 95% ate the salad bar in mid-October. A case-control study compares to non-ill students. Among 30 cases, 28/30 ate salad bar; among 50 controls, 15/50 ate salad bar. OR?
steps.reveal: OR = (28×35)/(2×15) = 980/30 ≈ 32.7. Strong evidence salad-bar exposure is associated. Combined with epi-curve timing + biological plausibility (hep A is faeco-orally transmitted via contaminated food, often produce), salad bar contamination is the working hypothesis.

steps.prompt: Step 9-10: refining + control. What follow-up would you do?
steps.reveal: Trace-back: test salad-bar food handlers for asymptomatic hep A infection (hep A often shed before symptoms). Trace produce supplier. Inspect food prep. Intervention: (a) issue **post-exposure prophylaxis** (hep A vaccine or immune globulin within 14 days of exposure) to potentially exposed but not yet infected students; (b) close + sanitize salad bar; (c) reinforce hand hygiene; (d) communicate publicly + via campus health. Mandatory hep A reporting at county + state public-health departments. Many real outbreaks have been traced to single asymptomatic food handlers in this pattern.

question.question: Why did wastewater surveillance for SARS-CoV-2 become a critical surveillance stream during the pandemic?
options: It is the only valid way to detect COVID-19.

It captures population-level shedding without depending on testing behavior; it is a leading indicator (shedding precedes symptoms + healthcare-seeking); it covers everyone in the catchment regardless of insurance, healthcare access, or symptoms; it scales cheaply once infrastructure is in place. Trade-offs: cannot identify individuals; signal noisy in small catchments; interpretation requires lab calibration.
question.explanation:
Wastewater surveillance scaled rapidly because:

(1) **Independent of testing behavior**. When clinical testing dropped (people stopped testing, at-home tests didn't report), wastewater kept measuring. Critical for detecting variant waves.

(2) **Leading indicator**. SARS-CoV-2 RNA is shed 1-2 days before symptoms; wastewater signal precedes clinical cases by ~5 days typically.

(3) **Population-scale denominator**. Captures the whole sewershed, including asymptomatic + people who never test. Eliminates the bias from differential testing access.

(4) **Variant detection via sequencing**. Wastewater sequencing detects variants days/weeks before clinical samples accumulate.

Limitations: cannot identify individuals; small communities have noisy signal; viral shedding kinetics vary by variant; calibration to case counts is imperfect. Still, CDC's NWSS now covers ~140 million Americans + provides a real-time public-health signal that complements clinical testing.

Generalization: wastewater also detects polio (a key tool for global polio eradication), RSV, mpox, influenza. The field has been transformed since 2020.

slides.workedSolution: Wastewater captures pre-symptomatic shedding + everyone in catchment without depending on testing access. Leading indicator (~5 days before clinical), population-scale denominator, scalable, useful for variant tracking. Limits: no individual ID, noisy in small catchments, calibration tricky. Now widely used for polio, RSV, mpox, flu in addition to COVID.

question.question: A foodborne outbreak investigation finds: 60% of cases ate vanilla ice cream; 40% of controls ate vanilla ice cream. Should you immediately conclude ice cream is the source?
options: Not yet. Compute the OR (~2.25) + test the difference statistically. But also: many foods are correlated; vanilla ice cream may simply be a proxy for the actual contaminated food. Look at attack-rate ratios for *all* foods together; the food with the highest AR-among-exposed combined with the lowest AR-among-unexposed is the most likely source.
No, ice cream is never a source of outbreaks.
Yes, but only if cases are female.
question.explanation:
60% vs 40% ⇒ OR ≈ 2.25 (or RR ≈ 1.5 if outcome's not rare). Statistically detectable in a moderate sample, but **moderate effect size**.

In outbreak investigation, the *index of suspicion* for a food source is highest when:
• AR among consumers is high (>50% typical).
• AR among non-consumers is low (<20% typical).
• The ratio is large (RR > 3 or OR > 5).
• Biology + epi-curve timing match.

A 60%/40% split is suspicious but weak. In foodborne investigations, the actual contaminated food often shows attack rates like 80%/15% — a much larger ratio. Vanilla ice cream might just be co-served with the actual contaminated item.

The analytic step is: compute attack rates for *every* food. The one with the largest, most discriminating ratio (+ biological plausibility, + matching incubation timing) is the leading hypothesis. Multivariable logistic regression with all foods controls for correlations.

Real example: a salmonella outbreak in 1985 implicated ice cream initially, but tracing showed contaminated lecithin. Tracing the supplier — not just the served food — closes the gap from suspicion to confirmation.

hints: What's the OR? Is it big?
slides.workedSolution: 60/40 split gives OR ≈ 2.25 — modest. Outbreak attack rates of the true source are typically 80%/15% or larger. Co-served foods are correlated; the implicated food may be a proxy. Solution: compute AR for all foods, find the one with highest AR ratio + biological plausibility, then trace supply chain.

question.question: In an outbreak of 200 cases over 4 weeks in a city of 2,000,000, what's the cumulative attack rate?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, walk through how you would investigate a cluster of 8 mysterious pneumonia cases in adults from the same office building over 2 weeks. What's your top-line plan?
question.rubric: Mentions: (1) confirm outbreak — 8 in 2 wks at one location exceeds expected; (2) establish case definition (clinical + spatial + temporal); (3) verify diagnoses with lab (Legionella urinary antigen would be high on differential for office cluster — recall Philadelphia 1976); (4) construct line list — onset, age, location in building, smoking, exposures; (5) descriptive epi — common-source vs propagated; (6) environmental investigation — cooling towers, plumbing, HVAC; (7) hypothesis-driven cohort/case-control among employees; (8) analytic confirm with OR/RR; (9) trace + intervene (shock chlorination of water if Legionella confirmed); (10) report + communicate. Notes that Legionella is the historically most likely cause for office-building pneumonia clusters; air-conditioning + cooling-tower contamination drives most modern outbreaks. Closes by emphasizing public-health surveillance + reporting are mandatory.
